title: Exfiltration Over Web Service: Exfiltration to Text Storage Sites
shortTitle: Exfiltration Over Web Service: Exfiltration to Text Stora...
summary: Exfiltration to Text Storage Sites uses public paste services to park stolen data as plain text. The adversary posts content to a site such as pastebin[.]com through a web form or the site's application programming interface (API), often receiving a short URL that can be fetched later from anywhere. Paste sites are popular with developers, so the domain usually falls into a permissive browsing category and the transfer is protected by TLS. Several services add expiry timers, unlisted addresses and optional encryption, which hides the content from casual review and shortens the window in which evidence exists. Detection therefore leans on proxy, domain and flow telemetry rather than file inspection: outbound POST requests to paste endpoints from servers or from non developer workstations, command line tools posting to a paste API, unusually large pastes, and short URLs that later appear in beacons or in phishing messages. A defender separates abuse from legitimate use by the role of the source host, the volume posted, and whether any local tooling explains the request.

beginner.definition: Exfiltration over a web service means sending stolen data out through a normal internet service. This version uses a public text sharing site, where people paste code and notes. The stolen data is posted there as text and given back as a short link. The attacker opens that link later from any computer in the world.
beginner.whyItMatters: Text storage sites are free, fast and hard to block, because developers use them for real work every day. Attackers can post data and collect it later without owning any server. Short links are easy to hide inside emails or chat messages. If nobody watches these sites, small but valuable thefts such as lists of usernames or keys can pass unnoticed.
howItWorks: The attacker gathers data and turns it into text, such as comma separated values or a settings dump.
They post the text to a paste site through its web form or through its API, the machine friendly entry point.
The site then returns a short link that points to the stored text on its servers.
They may set an expiry time, so the content disappears and leaves less evidence behind for defenders.
Later, the attacker or another machine fetches the link and reads the stolen data back.
Some services also offer a password or encryption, which keeps the content hidden even from the site.
beginner.example: Think of a public noticeboard in a large train station. Anyone can pin a sheet of paper there and walk away. Another person can come hours later, read it and copy the details without ever speaking to anyone. Nobody checks who pinned the paper or why. Posting stolen text on a paste site is exactly that, except the noticeboard can be reached from any computer in the world.
takeaways: Paste sites are a normal developer tool, so judge the source host and the volume rather than the site alone.
A single outbound post can carry a whole user list, because text is compact and easy to hide.
Short links from these sites should be treated as suspicious when they appear inside other traffic.

objectives: Explain why text storage sites are attractive as a short term exfiltration channel.
Describe how posting through a web form differs from posting through an API.
Identify the proxy, domain and flow records that reveal paste site activity.
Explain how expiry settings and encryption reduce the evidence available to defenders.
Describe how to distinguish developer paste use from data theft on the same network.
